sections.overview: Anopheles maculipennis is a European mosquito and the nominal member of its namesake complex. Its close relatives differ in host choice and malaria-vector importance; this species has a comparatively minor role.
sections.identification: The grey-brown adult has dark wing scales grouped into spots and a pale terminal fringe patch. A taxonomic description reports a female wing about 5.1 mm long, not a body length. Male antennae are more feathery, but adult appearance cannot reliably separate this mosquito from its close relatives. Its eggs have darker crossbars than those of Anopheles messeae; egg examination or DNA is more reliable than adult appearance. No representative body length, height, width, mass, or comparable male and female measurements were located.
sections.habitat: Larvae use fresh water, often with algae or vegetation, including streams and irrigation channels where they tolerate more flow than some close relatives.
sections.diet: Females strongly prefer animal blood, particularly where livestock are present. They may bite people when mosquitoes are abundant or animal hosts scarce; some siblings are more human-oriented.
sections.behavior: Adults often rest in stables; winter dormancy varies, with feeding and egg-laying recorded in mild conditions but absent during colder periods.
sections.reproduction: Females lay separate floating eggs on water; their bars help distinguish siblings. The aquatic larva and pupa develop before the winged adult emerges.
sections.ecology: Close relatives include Anopheles atroparvus, Anopheles labranchiae and Anopheles messeae. Older records often used Anopheles maculipennis for this broader group, complicating comparisons of vector role and host choice.
sections.conservation: This species can contribute to malaria transmission, but its animal-focused feeding generally gives it a smaller vector role than some relatives.
